articles.content: Many storybooks incorporate messages about not giving up when faced with a challenge — something that perhaps isn’t surprising given that perseverance is an important factor for learning and long-term success . Young children will persist longer when parents speak about effort . Comments such as “you are trying so hard at this” have been shown to be more effective at keeping children on task compared to comments such as “you are so clever.” Young children can also learn about effort from watching others persist . In the Concordia University Literacy lab , we wondered whether these others could be fictitious storybook characters. This question has a special place for me, Marie-Hélène, in light of my own early reading experiences. In Grade 3, my first year being exposed to an English-language curriculum, I was one of three students struggling to read. I often complained of stomach upset and was picked up early, which amplified my problems. I fell even further behind. My parents, both teachers at the time, decided to tutor me themselves with The Little Engine That Could to help me learn to connect letters to sounds of words (what educators call “decoding”). They chose this book because they thought the message of the story would give me courage at the same time I was learning to read. Parents and teachers still choose books with the hopes of both teaching and inspiring children. But does the behaviour of children really change following an inspiring book? Improving vocabulary, understanding When Sophie Thinks She Can’t … by Molly Bang features a girl who realizes she can improve in math through effort. (Scholastic) Storybooks have long been associated with improving vocabulary and socio-emotional understanding. But very few studies have explored whether popular storybooks can impact children’s persistence. Psychology and brain science expert Amanda Haber and her colleagues were among the first to explore this area. They read short non-fiction stories to four- and five-year-old children that were written specifically for their experiment. The stories focused on scientists’ natural talent or on the setbacks they encountered while doing their life’s work. Surprisingly, children who heard success stories spent less time working on a difficult task than children who heard setback stories. Even more surprisingly, children who heard success stories persisted for less time than children who heard no stories at all. However, Haber’s study compared groups of children rather than the same children before and after listening to storybooks. This led us to wonder whether popular storybooks featuring persistent characters would result in an observable increase in persistence in older children. Selecting perseverance storybooks After the Fall: How Humpty Dumpty Got Back Up Again by Dan Santat re-imagines how Humpty Dumpty faced his fears. (MacMillan Publishers) We wanted to know whether parents and educators could purposefully select storybooks to teach children about perseverance, and whether reading those types of books would increase the effort children put into difficult tasks. To answer this question, we read commercially available storybooks aloud to 154 second- and third-grade students . Classrooms were randomly assigned to one of two types of storybook groups: “Struggle” storybooks, which featured a perseverance theme (such as After the Fall: How Humpty Dumpty Got Back Up Again by Dan Santat, Rosie Revere, Engineer by Andrea Beaty and When Sophie Thinks She Can’t … by Molly Bang). While reading these with children, we explained the meaning of words and phrases associated with perseverance: grit, persistence and growth mindset. “Wordplay” storybooks, featuring play with words : During these readings, we explained alliteration (when two or more words close together starts with the same sound, like “silly snake”), onomatopoeia (when a word sounds like its meaning, as in “buzz”) and homophones (words that sound the same with different meanings). In both the “struggle” and “wordplay” groups, the adult who was reading stopped at five pre-selected spots in the books to incorporate the explicit vocabulary (for example, “grit” while reading Rosie Revere or “homophones” while reading Dear Deer ). How children behaved before, after readings The first week, we conducted one-on-one sessions with each child to determine their baseline knowledge of all six vocabulary words and had them complete two difficult tasks (such as Tangram puzzles and difficult mazes). The second week, over three days, the classrooms that were assigned to the “struggle” group were read one perseverance-themed storybook per day and had the associated vocabulary explained to them. Those in the “wordplay” group had the same experience with associated storybooks. The following day, we re-asked the children the meaning of all six words, and had them complete similar difficult tasks. At this time and also at the pre-test, we recorded the time on task, number of attempts and task completion. We did this to see if there was a difference between the struggle or wordplay groups and if there was a difference at the individual level (the time a child time spent on task at pre-test versus 24 hours after the readings). Rosie Revere, Engineer by Andrea Beaty is about how failure can ultimately lead to success. (Abrams Books for Young Readers/Andrea Beaty) As we expected, the children learned only the vocabulary that was taught within their storybook group. Aligned with Haber’s results, we found that seven and eight-year-old children who heard the struggle stories persisted longer. They made new attempts and were more successful on many of the difficult tasks compared to the children who listened to the other stories. Importantly, listening to the wordplay stories did not reduce perseverance — it simply did not increase the effort they applied on the difficult tasks presented after listening to those storybooks. Reading and elaborating concepts So, can storybook characters in stories featuring perseverance themes teach children about perseverance? ‘The Little Engine That Could’ 90th Anniversary Edition by Wally Piper, illustrated by Dan Santat. (Penguin Random House) The result of our experimental study indicated that yes they can. Reading storybooks that focus on perseverance, and elaborating on those key concepts while reading, can help children learn related words and increase the effort they invest when presented with difficult tasks. The findings did not surprise me, Marie Hélène. More than 40 years later, I still sometimes repeat to myself “I think I can, I think I can” when trying to accomplish a physically or emotionally challenging task. As researchers, we are left to conclude that storybooks about characters who face challenges, when paired with target vocabulary instruction, offer educators and parents simple, accessible and practical tools to help children develop their understanding of persistence. articles.content: Amazon workers in Delta, B.C. recently made labour history when they secured their first collective agreement with the company. The agreement is the first for Amazon workers anywhere in North America, according to Unifor , and only the second time Amazon workers in Canada have successfully unionized. Amazon workers in Laval, Que. , unionized in 2024, becoming the first in the country to do so, before Amazon announced that it would close all seven of its facilities in the province. The achievement in B.C. follows a lengthy battle with Amazon involving findings of employer interference during the organizing drive and a three-year collective agreement imposed by an arbitrator after negotiations failed. The case illustrates both the challenges of collective bargaining and the role Canadian labour laws can play in promoting and protecting workers’ rights. Remedial certification Workers at Amazon’s YVR2 warehouse in Delta first applied for union certification in 2024. However, the vote results were sealed pending an unfair labour practice complaint filed by the union, which alleged Amazon had attempted to dilute support for unionization by launching a hiring spree during the organizing drive. In its July 2025 decision, the B.C. Labour Relations Board found that Amazon’s non-salaried workforce at YVR2 had increased from 664 employees in January 2024 to 878 in June, an increase of more than 32 per cent. Based on witness testimony, written messages and other evidence, the board concluded that Amazon had “engaged in unnecessary hires for the purpose of interfering with the union’s organizing drive.” The board also found that Amazon committed additional unfair labour practices by engaging in “a pervasive anti-union campaign.” Given the seriousness of this conduct, the board determined that it would be “difficult to ascertain the true wishes of the employees through any other means.” It therefore ordered remedial certification . This exceptional remedy allows a labour board to certify a union without relying on a conventional employee vote. It is available under Section 14 of B.C.’s Labour Relations Code for serious cases in which an employer’s conduct has undermined the integrity of the standard voting or certification process. It is an important tool for labour boards, particularly in circumstances where the employer’s conduct and broader context suggest that even if workers subsequently vote against unionization, the result may reflect the employer’s influence rather than the workers’ genuine wishes or opinions. The board’s willingness to use this remedy in the Amazon case demonstrates that labour laws can protect and uphold workers’ rights. However, these additional layers of protection are reserved for exceptional circumstances. Securing a first collective agreement Union certification is a significant milestone, but it is only the beginning of collective bargaining. Once certified, a union must negotiate a first collective agreement with the employer. The structure and content of labour laws can be a significant help or hindrance at this stage. For example, although Amazon workers at a Staten Island warehouse in New York unionized in 2022, they still do not have a collective agreement in place. In April, the U.S. National Labor Board ordered Amazon to recognize the union and begin bargaining . The dispute has continued through the courts. Across most Canadian provinces, including B.C., the laws are structured to avoid significant delays in achieving a first collective agreement. Read more: Why did Amazon workers win the fight to form a union in Staten Island but not in Alberta? Recognizing that negotiating a first collective agreement can be particularly challenging, labour relations statutes across Canada contain provisions allowing for third-party intervention, such as mediation or arbitration, to help bring negotiations to a conclusion. Following the unionization of workers at YVR2 and unsuccessful negotiations, the Labour Relations Board ordered the first collective agreement to be settled through arbitration. The union served notice to bargain in October 2025, and a mediator was appointed in March 2026 to facilitate negotiations. By June, the mediator had concluded he could not recommend terms likely to be accepted by both sides, and recommended binding arbitration. The union accepted the recommendation, while Amazon rejected it. The Labour Relations Board then ordered the parties to conclude their first collective agreement through arbitration. The arbitrator imposed the three-year agreement on Nov. 13 of this year. Protecting bargaining rights Rules governing the collective bargaining process — including who is involved, how long it may take and the mechanisms available to conclude the negotiations — are necessary to ensure workers’ rights to unionize are upheld. These safeguards help ensure that unionization leads to its intended outcome: allowing workers to negotiate their terms and conditions of employment collectively with their employer. Having the terms of a collective agreement imposed by an arbitrator is far from ideal, but it’s sometimes necessary, particularly when an employer has fostered a hostile relationship with the union it must negotiate with. Ultimately, the B.C. Amazon workers’ case illustrates how difficult unionization and collective bargaining can be. It also demonstrates the important tools and safeguards built into Canada’s labour laws to promote and protect workers’ rights. Bethany Hastie receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada, the Canadian Foundation for Legal Research, and Queen's University. She is the Director of the Centre for Law in the Contemporary Workplace at Queen's University, and is a board member at Community Legal Assistance Society of BC.

The union served notice to bargain in October 2025, and a mediator was appointed in March 2026 to facilitate negotiations. By June, the mediator had concluded he could not recommend terms likely to be accepted by both sides, and recommended binding arbitration. The union accepted the recommendation, while Amazon rejected it. The Labour Relations Board then ordered the parties to conclude their first collective agreement through arbitration. The arbitrator imposed the three-year agreement on Nov. 13 of this year. Protecting bargaining rights Rules governing the collective bargaining process — including who is involved, how long it may take and the mechanisms available to conclude the negotiations — are necessary to ensure workers’ rights to unionize are upheld. These safeguards help ensure that unionization leads to its intended outcome: allowing workers to negotiate their terms and conditions of employment collectively with their employer. Having the terms of a collective agreement imposed by an arbitrator is far from ideal, but it’s sometimes necessary, particularly when an employer has fostered a hostile relationship with the union it must negotiate with. Ultimately, the B.C. Amazon workers’ case illustrates how difficult unionization and collective bargaining can be. It also demonstrates the important tools and safeguards built into Canada’s labour laws to promote and protect workers’ rights. articles.content: An educator at the Sunshine Coast Seed Saving Collective Workshop in September 2025 in Sechelt, B.C. (Tammara Soma) , CC BY-NC-ND A viral 2017 poll claimed that seven per cent of American adults believe chocolate milk comes from brown cows. The results drew a lot of laughs, along with criticism of the poll’s accuracy. But nearly a decade later, the results still raise an important question: How much do people really know about where their food comes from and how it’s grown? Grocery prices are skyrocketing in Canada amid a series of crises, from the lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic to global conflict, climate change and cyberattacks on grocery chains. As these events disrupt food supplies, it’s time to revisit a skill set humans have valued for millennia — food literacy . Knowing how to grow, harvest, hunt, process and cook our own food can help us become more self-sufficient, and it starts with learning from the land. Our disconnection from food The disconnect between the food we eat and the land can be explained by the concept of distancing . It also involves complex power dynamics, financing and entities in the global food system that make our food hard to understand. Distancing shapes how we value our food, the Earth and the people who work in the food system. Indigenous scholars Linda Clarkson and Vern Morrissette, along with Gabriel Régallet, argue that when we are separated from the source of our sustenance , we lose sight of “our responsibility and our kinship to the Earth.” In essence, we collectively forget our responsibilities to the land. For many Indigenous communities, food can no longer serve as medicine in the way it once did because colonization and the residential school system turned it into a tool of control. These systems forcibly disrupted intergenerational knowledge transfer, removed people from their lands, stigmatized traditional food and knowledge and ruptured relationships that had sustained people for generations. While many initiatives now offer students and adults opportunities to learn traditional food knowledge , these efforts are not yet mainstream. Building resilience through land-based learning One approach to addressing collective forgetting and reclaiming food knowledge is land-based learning, an Indigenous approach to teaching rooted in understanding the land as a teacher. In our ongoing project , “Countering Collective Forgetting: The Role of Land Based Learning,” we showcase the important work of those who teach these skills and how they are often undervalued. Through hands-on teaching, land-based learning encourages adaptive knowledge often gained through the wisdom of Elders. Our research team recently reviewed 137 land-based learning studies . We found that Elder-led mentorship was the most prevalent approach to learning, appearing in 73 per cent of the studies. To showcase how land-based learning works in practice, we conducted our study on the unceded territories of the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish) and shíshálh (Sechelt) Nations in an area commonly known as the Sunshine Coast of British Columbia. This region is particularly vulnerable to drought, and residents rely on ferry services for 60 per cent of their food, with 40 per cent coming from private barges and transport. We participated in five land-based learning activities, hosted one learning circle and interviewed eight local land-based learning practitioners. These practitioners included seed savers, farmers, permaculturalists, Indigenous Knowledge Keepers, chefs, school teachers and outdoor educators. They comprised a mix of Indigenous and settler residents in their communities. Our initial findings suggest that food acts as a form of living memory, held and reproduced through stories, relationships and also through engaging with the land. Graphic recording results from the ‘Learning from the Land’ Learning Circle, Nov. 9, 2025, Sechelt, B.C. (Fuselight Creative) , CC BY-ND The land is a teacher, healer During our learning circle, Alfonso Salinas, a shíshálh educator and cultural ambassador, opened the session with a song and prayer. He described how he was “taken under the wings” of Elders and of shíshálh Nation educator Candace Campo (xets’emits’a), co-founder of Talaysay Tours , a local Indigenous land-based learning and tourism company. On forest walks, Salinas learned how to use traditional plants and cedar as medicine. He shared his concerns about climate change and how invasive species are increasingly out-competing native plants such as salmon berries. His message was to never forget to teach the history of the land. One important piece of history shared by educators from the Sunshine Coast Seed Saving Collective during a seed workshop in September 2025 was that of the Japanese internment camps. They helped people remember and honour survivors by planting Slocan peas. Slocan peas are connected to Japanese Canadian families who were interred in the interior of B.C. during the Second World War. Slocan peas grew through a period of injustice, carrying a memory of adaption and resilience. Growing them is a form of healing. One educator who identified as Red River Métis shared that it’s hard to learn from the land when colonial policies continue to create barriers for Indigenous Peoples. Zoning rules, the reserve system and resource extraction projects all stand in the way. Finally, while many of the practitioners volunteered their time out of love, they also recognized this approach isn’t sustainable. Cost was a significant barrier for Robin, a settler who runs farm camps where kids from kindergarten to Grade 12 can learn how to grow, process and cook food. She said it was difficult to balance the need to create more affordable land-based learning programs while ensuring that practitioners can continue to teach. “Land-based educators should be paid fair wages,” she said. Supporting traditional food knowledge Seeds, like knowledge, don’t stay viable forever. They have to be planted, harvested, saved and shared for the cycle to continue. Knowledge from land-based learning carries on the the same way, as each generation of learners teaches the next. That cycle can help counter collective forgetting in our food systems, but only if those who dedicate their hearts and time to it have the space, fair wages and support they need. If we want to close the gap between ourselves and the food we eat, land-based learning offers an important path. To keep traditional food knowledge alive and make our food systems more resilient, we must value the wisdom that allows food to serve as medicine. That work begins by reconnecting with the land and with one another. articles.content: Teachers need time, professional learning and opportunities to develop approaches to AI that reflect their classroom contexts. (Pexels/Jessica Olivella) Artificial intelligence has entered education at a speed we have never experienced with any other technology. School boards are releasing AI policies , universities are revising academic integrity guidelines and students are experimenting with AI tools faster than educators can respond. But inside classrooms, a quiet tension is growing among educators. In 2025, with associate professor Rahul Kumar , I surveyed secondary school teachers across Ontario about their experiences with generative AI (GenAI). As a former secondary teacher and a current researcher who has examined leveraging digital techology , cell phones and AI to foster student engagement and learning , I was eager to see educator responses to the proliferation of AI in classrooms. The study was supported by Brock University and the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation . Of the 441 teachers who participated in the survey, 224 chose to respond to the optional final open response question inviting participants to share additional perspectives. Survey responses revealed students are far ahead of teachers with AI use, and teachers do not agree on when, how or even whether AI should be used in classrooms . They also highlighted a divide between educators who see AI as something that needs to be engaged and others who discussed their hesitation at length. A diversity of experiences, views Students are already regularly using AI . In our survey, 90.7 per cent of teachers reported direct knowledge of students using GenAI for academic work. Many educators are still figuring out what AI even is . Only 15.9 per cent of surveyed teachers rated their own GenAI proficiency as advanced or expert. Read more: The release of AI chatbots has harmed teens’ learning and Canada needs to act Educators view AI as a powerful tool, yet they differed in how they understand what this means for classroom learning. One wrote: “I think it’s naive to think AI isn’t going to play a central role in the lives of all students currently in school. We would be doing a disservice to students to not assist in preparing them to use these tools in their day-to-day lives.” Others framed their hesitation to use AI in the classroom as a matter of academic integrity: “AI, as it exists, is a tool to allow students to cheat, both on their work and themselves out of true learning.” Another said: “AI is NOT needed in education. Students already rely too much on technology.” Another captured the feeling of inevitability: “I think trying to ban the use of GenAI in schools is pointless — it is here to stay.” This person also said that schools, administrators and teachers “need to determine our way forward at this point.” Worry of losing what makes us human Among the responses, some teachers raised concerns about student thought and the authenticity of their work. Others questioned how AI might affect teacher expertise and their professional responsibilities. Educators who expressed resistance frequently focused on the erosion of cognitive thinking, authorship and authenticity. One wrote: “The one-to-one connection from student to product cannot be altered, added to or enhanced by AI because it will take away from the cognitive improvement in the student.” Another wrote: “I think it’s disheartening that so much emphasis is being placed on using GenAI in an institution where our strongest hope is to teach students to use critical thinking.” These comments suggest that, for some educators, the concern extends beyond the technology itself to what students may lose when AI takes over parts of the thinking and learning process. Others raised concerns about teachers’ intellectual and professional roles: “If teachers are using AI to create lessons and to complete academic work, what happens to the integrity of our profession?” This concern raises questions about teachers’ professional autonomy. Decisions about whether AI is appropriate depend on the subject being taught, students’ needs and the learning being assessed. Our broader survey findings reinforce the importance of preserving teachers’ judgment. Translating principles into practice Teachers have been positioned as the front-line decision-makers for AI integration , often under policy frameworks created without teacher consultation. School systems face legitimate questions about student privacy, academic integrity and appropriate AI use . But translating these broad principles into everyday teaching decisions is complex. A teacher must determine, for example, whether students can use AI to brainstorm ideas, revise their writing or generate portions of an assignment — and how to assess what students have actually learned. For teachers, these principles raise practical questions like: How can AI be incorporated without replacing student thinking? What constitutes acceptable assistance rather than inappropriate substitution? How can teachers determine whether the work submitted reflects a student’s understanding? Our survey suggests teachers need substantially more support. More than half of respondents (56 per cent) strongly agreed that teachers need time to integrate GenAI, while 43 per cent strongly agreed training is necessary. One participant captured the frustration, saying: “Our [school] board is already pushing us to use AI … but has not provided ANY guidelines or training as to how/when/why to use it.” They added that they “would love some guidance.” A policy problem that needs a grassroots solution Ontario school boards are beginning to establish expectations for AI use. For example, the Halton District School Board’s guidelines address student privacy, academic integrity and the teacher-directed use. Similarly, the Toronto Catholic District School Board provides guidelines for responsible AI use, including privacy safeguards and expectations for students and educators. While these establish important safeguards, teachers must still determine when and how AI supports learning in their classrooms. Teachers therefore need time, professional learning and opportunities to develop approaches that reflect their contexts. What’s at stake if we do nothing The divide between educators who believe AI shouldn’t have a place in high school classrooms and those who embrace it may shape the future of learning as much as the technology itself. If resistance wins, AI risks becoming another forbidden technology — with students using it secretly, without guidance ( something now emerging across sectors ). In this case, inequities in access and effective use will grow. If readiness wins, AI can extend rather than outsource thinking , assessment can emphasize inquiry and reflection and teachers can lead the conversation rather than react to it. Readiness is a systemic responsibility and the key to narrowing the divide. It should not be left as an individual burden. articles.content: Earlier this year, a British Columbia man — Seth Justin Christian — elected to be tried by a judge alone on one count of bestiality. The charge stems from an alleged incident in January at Abigail Equestrian, a horse-jumping and training business in Vernon, B.C. The charge has not been proven in court. His trial is set to begin in May 2027. If a B.C. judge convicts him under Section 160 of the Criminal Code , Christian could face up to 10 years in prison, a ban on owning animals and an order to pay compensation. He would also likely be added to the National Sex Offender Registry . The owner of Abigail Equestrian told CBC News that although the incident disgusted her and her clients, she expects her horses “will be OK physically and mentally.” Now compare that with what the law says about outright cruelty. Someone who beats a horse to death would face a maximum of five years in prison under Section 445 of the Code , part of a section titled “Wilful and Forbidden Acts in Respect of Certain Property.” The disparity between those penalties highlights the persistence of an ancient Judeo-Christian taboo in a society that thinks of itself as secular and modern. And the wide coverage of this case shows that an allegation of breaking this taboo still provokes disgust, fascination and even amusement. As a researcher on how literature and culture shape human attitudes toward nature, animals and the environment, I argue that not only is the prohibition on bestiality not new, but it has nothing to do with animal welfare. An ancient taboo turned law Leviticus 20 demands death for both the human and the animal involved. Christian theology later grouped bestiality and sodomy as non-procreative sins “against nature.” English law codified the sin in Henry VIII’s Buggery Act of 1533 , which made “the detestable and abominable vice of buggery committed with mankind or beast” a capital crime. The act conflated sex between men and sex with animals into a single offence. Canada inherited that law and kept the death penalty for buggery until 1865, when the Province of Canada (now Ontario and Québec) reduced it to life imprisonment . In 1967, a century later, then-Justice Minister Pierre Trudeau introduced and defended the government’s progressive Bill C-150, declaring that “there’s no place for the state in the bedrooms of the nation.” When the bill passed in 1969, Canada decriminalized buggery in private between consenting adults . Read more: Why animal orgasm matters to our moral universe A debate full of contradictions Kennels and stables were a different matter: Canada retained its bestiality law and, over time, toughened the punitive statute, making it a registrable sex crime in 2019 through Bill C-84 . Many European countries took a different path; most had stopped punishing bestiality in the 1960s and ‘70s , though a number have recriminalized it in the past two decades . But the debate over this ancient taboo, in Canada as elsewhere, is riddled with contradictions and shaky arguments. For example, animal activists insist that animals cannot consent to sex, but as philosopher Margret Grebowicz argues : “When animals appear as willing participants in these acts […] the question of consent becomes complicated. We know that they say no, but it is much less thinkable that they might say yes.” In any case, few of us query the consent of companion animals to be cuddled, confined or euthanized. Bill C-84 also closed a loophole exposed in 2016, when the Supreme Court of Canada upheld a child abuser’s acquittal on a bestiality charge because no penetration was involved. Parliament responded by redefining bestiality as “any contact, for a sexual purpose, with an animal.” That wording bans non-penetrative sexual activity while leaving farmers free to masturbate male livestock, including horses, to collect semen and artificially inseminate the females, none of which the animals consent to either . Bestiality in fiction Modern campaigns to criminalize bestiality have made allies of animal-welfare activists and conservatives who want to affirm the boundary between humans and animals. Rarely, small groups of “zoophiles” who say they “don’t do anything that the animal doesn’t want” speak out in defence of their sexuality. It is a polarized, morally charged debate. Bestiality and zoophilia even infiltrated Canadian literature in the form of Marian Engel’s Bear , which won the 1976 Governor General’s Literary Award for English-language fiction . It tells the story of a lonely archivist named Lou who is sent to catalogue an old library on an island in northern Ontario. There, she has an explicitly sexual relationship with a tame black bear. Far from feeling polluted by her bestial contact, Lou feels “clean and simple and proud” at the end of the novel. Zoophiles have few public advocates, and I’m certainly not one of them. Still, Bear shows how far our feelings about intimacy across species can drift from what the law permits. The next frontier of intimacy Today we find ourselves in an unsettling new epoch of artificial intimacy. People marry chatbots , writers imagine sexbots in need of liberation and movies like Ex Machina and I’m Your Man probe the boundary of human-android relationships. If the law still can’t say coherently why one kind of sexual contact with a horse is a crime and another is standard farm practice, it is poorly prepared for what comes next. Our ethics, politics and law lag far behind. And this reveals the futility of trying to police one of our oldest taboos by instinct rather than principle. If a B.C. judge convicts him under Section 160 of the Criminal Code , Christian could face up to 10 years in prison, a ban on owning animals and an order to pay compensation. He would also likely be added to the National Sex Offender Registry . The owner of Abigail Equestrian told CBC News that although the incident disgusted her and her clients, she expects her horses “will be OK physically and mentally.” Now compare that with what the law says about outright cruelty. Someone who beats a horse to death would face a maximum of five years in prison under Section 445 of the Code , part of a section titled “Wilful and Forbidden Acts in Respect of Certain Property.” The disparity between those penalties highlights the persistence of an ancient Judeo-Christian taboo in a society that thinks of itself as secular and modern. And the wide coverage of this case shows that an allegation of breaking this taboo still provokes disgust, fascination and even amusement. As a researcher on how literature and culture shape human attitudes toward nature, animals and the environment, I argue that not only is the prohibition on bestiality not new, but it has nothing to do with animal welfare. An ancient taboo turned law Leviticus 20 demands death for both the human and the animal involved. Christian theology later grouped bestiality and sodomy as non-procreative sins “against nature.” English law codified the sin in Henry VIII’s Buggery Act of 1533 , which made “the detestable and abominable vice of buggery committed with mankind or beast” a capital crime. The act conflated sex between men and sex with animals into a single offence. Canada inherited that law and kept the death penalty for buggery until 1865, when the Province of Canada (now Ontario and Québec) reduced it to life imprisonment . In 1967, a century later, then-Justice Minister Pierre Trudeau introduced and defended the government’s progressive Bill C-150, declaring that “there’s no place for the state in the bedrooms of the nation.” When the bill passed in 1969, Canada decriminalized buggery in private between consenting adults . Read more: Why animal orgasm matters to our moral universe A debate full of contradictions Kennels and stables were a different matter: Canada retained its bestiality law and, over time, toughened the punitive statute, making it a registrable sex crime in 2019 through Bill C-84 . Many European countries took a different path; most had stopped punishing bestiality in the 1960s and ‘70s , though a number have recriminalized it in the past two decades . But the debate over this ancient taboo, in Canada as elsewhere, is riddled with contradictions and shaky arguments. For example, animal activists insist that animals cannot consent to sex, but as philosopher Margret Grebowicz argues : “When animals appear as willing participants in these acts […] the question of consent becomes complicated. We know that they say no, but it is much less thinkable that they might say yes.” In any case, few of us query the consent of companion animals to be cuddled, confined or euthanized. Bill C-84 also closed a loophole exposed in 2016, when the Supreme Court of Canada upheld a child abuser’s acquittal on a bestiality charge because no penetration was involved. Parliament responded by redefining bestiality as “any contact, for a sexual purpose, with an animal.” That wording bans non-penetrative sexual activity while leaving farmers free to masturbate male livestock, including horses, to collect semen and artificially inseminate the females, none of which the animals consent to either . Bestiality in fiction Modern campaigns to criminalize bestiality have made allies of animal-welfare activists and conservatives who want to affirm the boundary between humans and animals. Rarely, small groups of “zoophiles” who say they “don’t do anything that the animal doesn’t want” speak out in defence of their sexuality. It is a polarized, morally charged debate. Bestiality and zoophilia even infiltrated Canadian literature in the form of Marian Engel’s Bear , which won the 1976 Governor General’s Literary Award for English-language fiction . It tells the story of a lonely archivist named Lou who is sent to catalogue an old library on an island in northern Ontario. There, she has an explicitly sexual relationship with a tame black bear. Far from feeling polluted by her bestial contact, Lou feels “clean and simple and proud” at the end of the novel. Zoophiles have few public advocates, and I’m certainly not one of them. Still, Bear shows how far our feelings about intimacy across species can drift from what the law permits. The next frontier of intimacy Today we find ourselves in an unsettling new epoch of artificial intimacy. People marry chatbots , writers imagine sexbots in need of liberation and movies like Ex Machina and I’m Your Man probe the boundary of human-android relationships. If the law still can’t say coherently why one kind of sexual contact with a horse is a crime and another is standard farm practice, it is poorly prepared for what comes next. Our ethics, politics and law lag far behind. And this reveals the futility of trying to police one of our oldest taboos by instinct rather than principle.
